MR. COATES  REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING CLOSURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting all hon. members of the house. Yesterday I posed the following question to the Prime Minister:
Did the right hon. gentleman state in the course of a press conference in Vancouver on September 17 that closure would be used if the flag committee did not come forward with a near unanimous decision?
To this question I received this emphatic reply from the Prime Minister:
No such statement was made.
I now have available to me the transcript of the Prime Minister's press conference at Vancouver on September 17, which on page 15 contains the following question and reply: If you do face the problem seriously of continued filibuster in your minority position, how long can a government tolerate it without going to the people to get a clear cut decision of the parliamentary majority and parliamentary reform?
To which the Prime Minister replied:
It is not essential to go to the people in order to stop a filibuster. There are rules for that purpose. They are used as a last resort, but they are there, and they have been kept there by the previous government, so the previous government must have felt it was unwise to take out the closure rule. It is still there, but I don't like to see legislation enacted by closure. It is much better to do it some other way.
As a result of this statement many newspapers across Canada informed their readers that the Prime Minister threatened closure if the flag committee did not reach a satisfactory decision. Yesterday I mentioned the Montreal Star, which on September 18 carried a headline reading "Closure if Necessary-Pearson".
The Prime Minister's reply to me is not in keeping with the facts, and places the flag committee in the same position as the Prime Minister placed the House of Commons with the threat of a general election if his flag design were not accepted. I consider the Prime Minister owes the house an apology for this statement in Vancouver, and the flag committee a categorical retraction of the threat of closure so they might be able to continue their most important task in the proper atmosphere.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting all members of the house, and in particular the members of the special committee on procedure and organization which is under Your Honour's chairmanship.
Yesterday a press release was issued by the New Democratic party dealing with that party's proposals for the reform of parliament. The committee on procedure and organization, which is a committee of this parliament, has been discussing the problem of the reform of parliament, and has long since agreed that it would try to come to an all party agreement on the proposals that it presented to parliament. Indeed, the representative of the New Democratic party on that committee was one of those who most strongly felt that, if possible, unanimity should be reached before our proposals were presented here.
I think it is an affront to this house, and in particular to the committee itself, that the party which had agreed there should, if possible, be an all party agreement before the committee's proposals for reform of this house were presented, should now break that agreement.
Shame.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. J. Robichaud (Minister of Fisheries):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it has been customary for the Minister of Fisheries, in introducing the estimates of his department, to give a brief resume of the state of Canada's fishing industry and of the fisheries resources, and to outline the current activities of the department. By doing this now, I may be answering in advance some of the questions which hon. members may have in mind. If there are points which I do not make sufficiently clear, I shall be glad to explain them in detail when we are considering the estimates of the department item by item.
Fishing is a risky and hazardous calling. Every year it takes its toll of lives. During the past year, while there has been no major tragedy, there have been isolated instances of men lost at sea or falling victim to the mishaps which are all too common in the lives of those whose work takes them to sea. I am sure every member of this house wiU join me in paying tribute to Canada's fishermen and their families. These are the people upon whose strength and skill the entire industry is built and, as you will note in the report which follows, it is a primary concern of the Department of Fisheries to see that they are employed as safely and profitably as possible.
I should like to make a few remarks about the up to date status of the fishing industry from an economic point of view. With the exception of the codfish catch from the trap fishery of Newfoundland, the 1964 season has been generally satisfactory. The first indication came with early fishing for spring salmon in British Columbia which yielded 4.9 million pounds during the first six months of 1964, compared with 3.6 million pounds for the same period in 1963. For the first seven months of this year, landings of all species by commercial fishermen on both coasts

totalled 1.2 billion pounds or 30 million pounds more than the landings in the first seven months of last year. This increase was registered despite a decline in the cod catch of 48 million pounds.
The value of the commercial catch is larger so far this year than the increase in landings would suggest. The increase in value to the end of July was about 20 per cent against 2 per cent increase in the volume of landings. This is accounted for principally by a higher proportion of the more valuable species in the total catch. In British Columbia, salmon landings are up by 34 million pounds, and in the Atlantic provinces there have been significant increases in the landings of haddock, small flat fish, swordfish and scallops. The figures just released yesterday for the month of August were most encouraging and show a further trend toward a record year for Canada's fisheries both in quantity and in value.
This expansion in output at the primary level of the industry occurred without any softening of dockside prices. In fact, in some cases the price level moved up over the record level set a year ago. The most spectacular price rise has taken place in the first sale of Newfoundland salted codfish. The short supply resulting from the disappointing trap fishery earlier in the season and competition from Newfoundland freezing plants has been reinforced by strong demands from the major markets. The result has been that Newfoundland fishermen are now getting the highest prices on record, especially for fish in the salt bulk form. If present prices hold through the balance of the season they may offset, on the over-all value of salted fish, the effect of the smaller production. An indication of the situation in the markets comes from the report that Norway, a traditional net exporter of salted fish, is purchasing a substantial quantity of salt bulk fish from Newfoundland. I still express the hope that a better late fall fishery in Newfoundland will bring the cod landings in that province close to normal.
In the maritime provinces the expansion in production and quality of swordfish and tuna, the last just a two year old industry, continues. I want to state here that tremendous improvement in the tuna fishery and processing is expected within the next few months, particularly in the southern section of New Brunswick. I want to take this opportunity to commend those who have been pioneers in this new fishery, Captains Matthews and Savage from Campobello island.

I should like also to mention here Captain Norman Ryall from the west coast, who has shown a special interest in the development of the tuna industry, and for whom the largest fishing boat ever built in North America will be launched in a few weeks time at one of the shipyards at Levis, Quebec.
The United States is the predominant market for these special species. This year the value of scallop landings is up by $900,000 and swordfish by $600,000 over the last season. The average price to the fisherman for these species in the first seven months of this year has been 42 cents per pound for scallops and 31 cents per pound for swordfish, both up slightly from 1963.
In British Columbia the good catches of spring salmon, to which I referred earlier, were followed by unexpectedly large catches of sockeye, which is the most valuable of the British Columbia salmon. Landings of this species during the current season were 17 million pounds, an increase of 10 million pounds over the disappointing catch of last year. By early September the sockeye pack stood at over 343,000 cases-almost double the pack of the same period of 1963. The sockeye run on the Skeena river was well above the earlier expectations which suggested that 300,000 of these fish might be taken. It now appears that the actual catch may be 2J times that number. Most of the major runs are expected to surpass the preseason forecasts.
The halibut catch, however, has been disappointing especially from area 2, but prices have firmed up considerably from last year. Mediums have been quoted at 27 to 28 cents a pound, which is about five cents higher than last year's level. Herring landings during the January-July period were below last year by about 13 million pounds, but higher prices maintained the value of the catch. The summer herring operation has yielded good results so far. Catches of the minor species, including the cods and soles, continue to expand and reached a total of 32 million pounds by the end of July, an increase over 1963 of 5 million pounds.
The quantity of fishery products exported in any January-July period include a large proportion of the production of the previous year with the exception, of course, of items sold alive or chilled. For this reason, export data at mid-year are not closely related to the level of production data covering the prior six months. The value of exports to the end of June, however, indicates a continuing strong demand for fishery products from this

Supply-Fisheries
country. For all products this figure for the six months period was $88 million, compared with $72 million to the end of June 1963. The United States continues to be the largest customer in this field and Canadian exporters sold $58 million worth out of the $88 million total to markets in the United States.
The demand for groundfish products continued without abatement. In the first six months of 1964 exports of fillets and blocks totalled 61 million pounds or about 60 per cent of United States imports of these commodities from all countries and an increase of 14 million pounds over the volume imported from Canada during the first six months of 1963. Iceland continues as a strong competitor in the field and is now supplying the United States with about 30 per cent of its import requirements. It is therefore most imperative that our fishermen as well as our processors exercise greater care and better attention in producing the best quality product possible.
The strong demand for Canadian fishery products, and especially that associated with the growing population on this continent, has been accompanied by firm or rising prices. This situation has been apparent for several years and the industry is reacting to it in significant development and expansion. This is particularly true on the Atlantic coast where heretofore capital formation from earnings within the industry was not the rule. The construction of the large plant at Lunenburg and the plans for development at Canso, Georgetown and Summerside are evidence of the optimism pervading the industry. The Atlantic fleet now includes 92 trawlers, most of which are modem and efficient. Five years ago this fleet comprised 53 vessels. This is an increase of 80 per cent, and most of the 53 were used ships which had been purchased from the United Kingdom and the United States. The scallop fleet now contains about 35 vessels over 75 feet in length, capable of exploiting distant beds and landing scallops of high quality. Five years ago there were only nine scallop vessels of this size on the Atlantic coast. Fishermen, alone or in partnerships, are acquiring vessels in the 45 to 65 foot class which fish near and middle distance waters. They are equipped with modern fish location and catching gear, and their owners are actively experimenting with new types of gear and new methods of fishing. Nearly 500 of these vessels have been purchased by fishermen with financial assistance provided by the Department of Fisheries in recent years.

Because of the importance of the subject and the wide interest in it, the matter of territorial limits merits some mention at this time. The Territorial Sea and Fishing Zone Act, proclaimed on July 23, established a 12 mile fishing zone around the coasts of Canada. This means an additional nine mile fishing zone has been added to the existing territorial sea limit of three miles. The act also authorized the governor in council to establish straight base lines from which the territorial sea could be measured. Until such time as the straight base lines are established, the additional nine mile fishing zone is to be measured from the existing territorial sea limits.
While taking this unilateral step of establishing the new fishing zone and proceeding to the establishment of straight base lines, the government initiated discussions with a number of friendly countries which have been fishing off our coasts, some of them for many centuries, to see how their interests might be affected.
We are now on the second round of these discussions with eight countries and hope that they may be concluded soon, at which time the government intends to proceed with the establishment of the new base lines. I wish I were in a position to give the house more details of the second phase of these negotiations, but I am confident that I will have the co-operation of all hon. members in recognizing that such details cannot be made available while negotiations of this nature are under way.
On the high seas, where fishing rights are not a question, there is still need for consultation and agreement with other countries for the protection of the resource itself. This calls for a joint management program entailing a great deal of research and some long range planning. For this reason a number of international fisheries commissions have come into being, and Canada is represented on seven. Four of them are established under multilateral agreements, and deal with the fisheries of the northwest Atlantic ocean, the fisheries of the north Pacific, the stocks of fur seals and of whales. The other three agreements under which joint commissions operate are between Canada and the United States and deal with Pacific sockeye and pink salmon of the Fraser river system, the halibut of the north Pacific ocean, and the fisheries of the great lakes.
In connection with one of the foregoing, the international convention for the high seas fisheries of the north Pacific ocean, we are

even now engaged here in Ottawa on a third round of talks between the three countries involved-Canada, Japan and the United States. The purpose of these talks, which are being conducted in a hopeful and cooperative atmosphere, is to find a better basis for resolving different views as a result of the experience gained during the 11 years the convention has been in operation. A new draft convention is being considered. Again, Mr. Chairman, I wish I were in a position to give more details of the negotiations which are now taking place here in Ottawa, but it would be improper for me to do so at this time.
I hope that at the conclusion of these negotiations I will be in a position to make a statement to the house. As I have said before, after an agreement is reached-and I have confidence that an agreement can be reached-I will refer to the standing committee on marine and fisheries the terms of this agreement before ratification.
I have already mentioned in this house our national fisheries development program the basis of which was set up at a federal-provincial conference on fisheries development which I convened in Ottawa last January. I explained, too, that this was also a forum for the views of industry as well as of government, since briefs were received at that time from the Fisheries Council of Canada and from fishermen's representatives from various areas.
The progress made as a result of this conference is quite heartening, and I think this is the proper time and place to report on it. A number of projects are now well under way as co-operative efforts between federal and provincial administrations. These include the following:
1.	The development and demonstration of trawls suitable for rough bottom, so that our Canadian fishermen can exploit grounds now being actively fished by foreign vessels.
2.	The modification of small boats for inshore dragging and introduction of Japanese-type mechanical squid jigging equipment- this is in the Newfoundland area.
3.	Demonstration of the construction and operation of the western or Pacific trawl in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick waters.
4.	The charter of a Norwegian whaling vessel, with her crew, to learn and to demonstrate the possibilities of reviving the whaling industry on the Atlantic coast.
5.	The improvement of trawling operations for ground-fish off the Pacific coast.

6.	A survey is being made of the Irish moss resources in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island and a few days ago I made the announcement that a site had been selected on Prince Edward Island for the construction, with assistance from the Atlantic development board, of an Irish moss drying plant.
7.	The exploration of a new scallop bed off Shippegan gully.
8.	Experimental and development work in Quebec on fish-finding gear towed by helicopter.
9.	The development and introduction of improved lobster processing line techniques in Quebec plants, and

During the conference it became obvious that there was a need for regional federal-provincial committees similar in concept to the federal-provincial Atlantic fisheries committee which was established in 1958 to coordinate programs for fisheries development, and the federal-provincial committee for Ontario fisheries. Consequently we now have a federal-provincial committee for British Columbia fisheries and a federal-provincial prairie fisheries committee. All these federal-provincial regional committees are of inestimable value in that they constitute formal consultative bodies which can discuss and deal with questions of common interest such as marketing, research and fisheries management generally. A sport fishery advisory committee has also been established in British Columbia.
Agreement has been reached to include officials of the departments of northern affairs and citizenship and immigration on the appropriate committees when subjects affecting Northwest Territories development are to be discussed.
Restriction of entry into the lobster fishery has been considered at regional federal-provincial meetings; so has the subject of limitation of entry into the Pacific salmon fisheries, and there have been discussions on fish farming, in particular, with respect to commercial trout farms. A good deal of background material on this subject has been prepared and these matters are under active consideration.
The control of pollution of our waters remains a subject of vital interest and much information has been collected. The fisheries research board has been in consultation with the national research council concerning the establishment of an intergovernmental committee on pollution to ensure the availability

Supply-Fisheries
of complete information. It is hoped that work on salt-water pollution in the Atlantic region can be started and that the work already carried out on the Pacific coast can be strengthened.
Discussions have taken place with the Department of Labour and with provincial authorities on vocational training and education for fishermen, and my department is creating an educational unit to co-ordinate activities in this connection.
Then again, as a result of recommendations made during the federal-provincial conference, a fisheries-related approach to improvements in harbour works has been discussed with the Department of Public Works and the Atlantic development board. Discussions have also taken place with the Department of Finance concerning improvements to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. The provincial authorities and the industry are being asked for their views concerning credit facilities for fishermen and possible inadequacies in the existing legislation.
In addition to the programs already mentioned, many other industrial development projects are under way. Powered gill-net haulers are being introduced, synthetic cod gill-nets are being tested in areas where they have not yet been used, and we are experimenting with synthetic materials for cod trap construction. We are also working on a prototype of a mechanized gillnet boat capable of multipurpose fishing operations, and we have introduced porbeagle shark fishing gear and techniques in the Atlantic provinces.
Modern methods of seining herring in western and southern Newfoundland also are being demonstrated to ascertain the commercial potential of such operations in those areas. New techniques in salt fish drying, using high speed equipment developed in the department, are being demonstrated on a commercial scale for the benefit of industry, and we are producing, on a pilot plant basis, commercially acceptable instant fish-potato flakes.
We are working on a design of a deep sea stern ramp trawler to meet the specific Canadian requirements for ground-fish trawling operations and are experimenting with an electrified trawl.
In Nova Scotia we are studying the distribution and abundance of herring, whiting, argentines and sandlaunce, which are species of small fish not yet exploited by Canadian fishermen. The object is to develop offshore trawling gear and techniques so that this

situation may be remedied. Scottish methods of Danish seining are being tested to increase the efficiency of this technique, and we are hoping to develop a distant water tuna fishery, using large seine boats.
A new and promising design for a plastic lobster trap is being tried out on a commercial scale in Prince Edward Island, where we also hope to encourage offshore herring seining methods, like those used in Iceland, in order to meet European orders for frozen herring. We are aware of the great potentialities of fishing for pelagic fish in the gulf of St. Lawrence and we are prepared to meet this challenge. Crab fishing operations are under way in the Northumberland strait, and we are hoping that a crab fishery can be developed around the Magdalen and Anticosti islands. We anticipate good results from a manually operated hydraulic clam digger developed by the fisheries research board for clam beds in the maritimes.
In British Columbia one of our aims is to diversify fishing operations off the Pacific coast by the introduction of better trawling operations for groundfish, and we are working on an improved refrigeration system for use in the halibut fishery in distant areas.
The foregoing are just some of the many projects by which the department hopes to aid all segments of the fishing industry in all areas by increasing the efficiency of the fleets, the gear and the techniques.
Significant advances have been made by industry in providing facilities to increase their processing capacity and to expand the variety of fish and shellfish products available to an increasingly quality conscious public. The department's program for the inspection of fish plants and fishery products to ensure the production of good quality fish under acceptable sanitary conditions will receive added impetus with the passing of regulations providing for the compulsory registration of fresh and frozen fish plants effective April 1, 1965. This will involve assessment of construction, equipment and processing procedures in some 260 plants across Canada. Initial registration will be granted when a plant meets specified minimum requirements in these categories. The eventual success of the program will depend upon active enforcement of the requirements through frequent plant visits by a well trained inspection staff.
Complementary to the development program for improved product quality at the processing level has been the department's work in the fields of fish boat inspection and

dockside grading. As an outcome of the federal-provincial conference on fisheries development, which pointed to the need for improvement in the quality of fish as landed, more emphasis has been placed on these aspects of inspection. Regulations are being developed for adequate sanitation and handling methods on fishing boats. Educational material is being prepared for the assistance of fishermen in handling and caring for their catch, and also for those handling fish at the retail level.
The department's laboratories are responsible for the inspection of domestic and imported canned fish; experimental work on the development of new and improved standards for canned and other types of fish; shellfish toxicity control programs; the bacteriological control of fresh and frozen shellfish plants and the purity of plant water supplies. These services are provided by permanent or mobile laboratories as the need dictates. In this connection it is proposed to replace the mobile laboratory facilities in northern New Brunswick with a permanent laboratory. We hope that this new laboratory which will be established at Shippegan in the centre of a 35 to 40 million pound yearly production will be in operation for the 1965 season.
Unsatisfactory water supplies for processing operations have been a major factor in a number of plants being unable to attain the Canadian government specifications board standards for approved plants, and this will undoubtedly be a factor in the plant certification program. Water supplies received attention in a number of briefs presented to the federal-provincial conference and it is encouraging to note that the Atlantic development board has taken an active interest in the matter of plant water supplies. Survey data, which may lead to the development of projects aimed at improving water supplies, are presently being reviewed. The department's laboratories will continue, and expand where necessary, participation in these surveys.

I have mentioned the education of fishermen, but we also have another educational program which extends right across the country, directed at consumers. The object, quite simply, is to get Canadians to eat more fishery products in the home, in restaurants and hotels and in institutions. Departmental home economists work out of test kitchens in the major centres, giving demonstrations of fish cookery and convincing more and more people of the value of fish as food. As a result of these demonstrations and by the use of various kinds of publicity, we distribute thousands of pieces of consumer literature every year, and the highly successful "Canadian Fish Cook Book" is recognized as a final authority-indeed, a United States publisher is even now inquiring about publication rights in that country. Film and filmstrips, produced for the department by the national film board, are widely circulated and in several instances have won international awards for excellence. Departmental publications, as well as displays and exhibits at conventions and meetings where fish is a relevant topic, are also used in our consumer educational program. Other printed or filmed educational material is produced directly for the benefit of the industry and the fishermen themselves.
As I stated at the beginning of this review, conditions in the fishing industry in 1964 have been encouraging. Prices generally have been satisfactory. However, price support was necessary to relieve a 1963 surplus production of sauger in the prairie provinces, where markets were weakened by a temporary reduction in the demand for

smoked fish. Assistance also was given by the fisheries prices support board to expand the markets for pickled herring, mackerel and alewives, following a curtailment of shipments during 1962 and 1963 due to political and economic difficulties in some of the Caribbean markets for these products.
The Newfoundland bait service is continuing its program of expansion and modernization. A new vessel, the C.G.S. Arctica was commissioned in July, has a larger capacity and greater storage space than its predecessor, and will provide bait service to many isolated communities in Newfoundland. In addition, two new trucks have been added to our facilities so that we can take advantage of the expanding highway network in the province. We are also making the most out of this year's run of squid so that we should be able to meet all the bait requirements of the coming year. In fact, instructions were recently issued to purchase an additional two million pounds of squid for storage for next year's bait requirements in Newfoundland, in addition to quantities of herring and capelin already in storage.
The department's fishermen's indemnity plan-which provides low cost insurance for small fishing vessels-continues to expand. At the present time more than 6,800 vessels, valued at about $25 million, are covered by this insurance scheme. We have initiated a study of the possibilities of extending the indemnity plan to the inland fisheries, as well as extending the scope of the operations to include fixed fishing gear and shore installations. It is expected that this study should be completed before the end of the year.
The scientific investigations which are vital to successful management of the fisheries are carried out by the fisheries research board of Canada, which is actively engaged in studies of aquatic animals in the three oceans that touch Canadian shores and in several of Canada's many lakes.
An appreciable amount of research is directed to meeting requirements of a number of international fisheries commissions. Investigations are carried out on fisheries technology aimed at improving the quality of fisheries products.
Among the highlights of the current year are the following:	20 authentic returns
of pink salmon have occurred to date in St. Mary's bay, Newfoundland, from 2.5 million eggs taken in British Columbia and transplanted in North Harbour river, Newfoundland in 1962. This number may seem small to

many of us, but I want to assure hon. members that it is quite significant to the scientists of the fisheries research board who are proceeding with this program. In fact, larger planting involving 10 million eggs is planned for this fall.
Progress has been made in studying the survival of young Pacific salmon in the sea with a view to predicting the abundance of major salmon runs. The important Atlantic fishing grounds were surveyed and valuable information obtained on the condition of various stocks of fish. The behaviour of fish is being studied as a basis for improving the design of fishing gear. Greenland cod have been found in moderate abundance in western coastal Arctic waters. The substance responsible for causing off-odours in Labrador cod fillets has been identified. Significant progress has been made in devising pumping equipment for unloading fish such as salmon. The process for preparing fish protein concentrate has been modified to permit use of a wider variety of fish.
Seventeen new research projects have arisen from deliberations at last January's federal-provincial fisheries development conference. On the Atlantic coast the main research emphasis will be on utilization of underexploited species-capelin, herring, sharks, tuna, swordfish, whiting, argentines, and others. Further work is also planned on lobsters, particularly on the prevention of losses in holding pounds, and intensive work is under way on various aspects of the processing of Newfoundland cod. On the Pacific coast, major efforts will be directed to studies of coho and chinook salmon in relation to sport and commercial fishing conflicts, and on increasing sockeye salmon production on the Skeena river.
Biological aspects of oceanographic research are being expanded to complement the growing program in physical oceanography by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. The board is playing a leading role in the establishment of an oceanographic information service which will provide background for fisheries forecasting.

I have tried in this review to cover the present situation of the fishing industry and to outline the work being carried out by my department. No doubt further questions will occur to hon. members as the items are considered, at which time I shall be happy to answer them.
Mr. Chairman, before resuming my seat I should like to repeat what I said yesterday in reply to a question regarding the killing of seals. This is an important matter to which reference has been made on several occasions during this present session and in respect of which there is general interest throughout this country. My department has received close to 2,000 letters concerning the seal operations. As I said yesterday, it is our intention to amend the regulations in this regard. A meeting was held on May 19 in Moncton with representatives of the industry, a number of fishermen and a representative of the humane society. The draft amendments have now been prepared and a second meeting will take place here in Ottawa on October 1. I was pleased that the minister mentioned the legislation passed by the house regarding the 12 mile limit, but I regret that so far as the general public are concerned there has been a great deal of misunderstanding about what the situation is. I recognize that the minister has not been particularly guilty in this regard, but in recent election campaigns some of his colleagues created the impression that immediately the government came to power our territorial waters would be extended to 12 miles and that conditions within that 12 mile area would be exactly the same as they have been within the historic three mile territorial sea where no foreigners fish.
I am pleased to note that the act has been brought into effect, but I note that an order in council was passed on July 17 which exempts the fishing vessels of a number of countries, the United States of America, France, Great Britain, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Norway and Denmark for the time being at least from the application of the legislation excluding foreign fishing vessels from the 12 mile territorial sea. I hope that at some time during the course of the minister's replies he will be able to give the committee some indication of what the policy of the government is going to be in this regard. If there is going to be a phasing out period for these countries, what are the terms going to be? Are some of these countries going to be excluded from the application of the act indefinitely, I hope the minister will be able to answer no. In actual fact the situation at the present time is much the same as it has been in previous years, with the exception that no additional foreign fishermen can come within the 12 mile limit.
I also hope that at an early date the government will be able to announce the co-ordinates to be established under this legislation which will close off large bodies of water and

make them national waters of Canada. I should like to think that this will be done before next spring. engine the Howay and Laurier, build a new Cygnus, also the Cape Freels, the A.T. Cameron, the G.B. I commend the minister for the interest he is showing in additional educational programs in co-operation with the provinces for fishermen, because this is a highly competitive international industry in which we cannot depend on having any built-in advantage so far as competition with other countries is concerned. We, in many cases, exploit a common resource upon the high seas. Therefore it is essential that the industry is engaged in by people who are of the highest skills and capabilities in order to compete effectively with the high standards of technical training which have been a common situation in Europe, and no doubt in Japan and the other countries with which Canada now competes. Of course the minister no doubt recognizes that the opportunities in this regard are greater than they were because of the great developments in the building of technical and other schools as a result of joint programs between the Department of Labour and the provinces over the last number of years.
I commend the minister for keeping his remarks non-political, because this is a nonpolitical department and we are all interested in its progress. Some statements that have been made by some of his colleagues during previous election campaigns are regrettable. Some of these statements indicated these people were not as knowledgeable as they should be with regard to the fishing industry, and it would seem evident they hoped they were speaking to an audience which was not very well versed in the problems of the fishing industry because they were trying to
Supply-Fisheries
create the impression that any difficulties of the fishing industry were due almost solely to the minister who happened to be the head of the department at the time. I hope that this sort of thing will not happen in the future. I take no official credit, but when I headed the department I had the honour of being the head of a department manned by some of the finest, most capable civil servants in Canada, and perhaps anywhere in this regard. I would say the main limitation on progress so far as the Department of Fisheries can initiate it and stimulate it, is chiefly lack of funds. There is no lack of technical knowledge, skill and desire concerning what is beneficial to the fishing industry. There have been unfortunate statements made in the past, as I have said, by some of the minister's colleagues.
I note that one of the items which has increased is the cost of publications and advertising. Perhaps the minister might consider running an advertisement in some of the newspapers in the fishing areas stating that the outlandish and extravagant promises made by some of his colleagues in the heat of election campaigns should not be taken seriously by the fishing industry.

Before you recognize the next hon. member, Mr. Chairman, may I correct now what I am sure the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) inadvertently overlooked. He stated the total amount by which the estimates were increased was $395,000. There is also an amount of $1,588,000 in the supplementary estimates, which makes the over-all increase $1,982,000.
I was aware of that. I was reading the comparison of the main estimates on the sheet in the back of the book.

At the outset of my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I find myself in complete agreement with both the minister and the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean), the former minister of the department, when they referred to the fact that most of the success so far achieved in enhancing the development of the fishing industry in Canada has resulted from the fact that we have a small but devoted band of public servants in the administrative and scientific areas of the department. I certainly wish to join with the minister and the previous speaker in expressing my appreciation, on behalf of this party, of the kind of service they have given to Canada and to Canadian fishermen in particular.

Supply-Fisheries
* The hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) suggested that this was not a political department. He made reference to some statements which apparently have been rankling him a little bit and which were made by members or former members of this house. I would agree with him that in the sense of the word "political", which was obvious from his remarks, by and large the Department of Fisheries has not been a political department. Nevertheless I would suggest that in the proper use of the term "politics", it is as much a political department as any other department of government and that questions of policy developed with the knowledge of our fishing resources present and potential, are very much matters of urgent political consideration in this country. They certainly should be of urgent consideration to the members in this house.
The minister in his statement gave us as comprehensive an outline of the activities of the department during the past year as I suppose one could expect from him in a single speech. Most of what he said, on the face of it, sounded as if there had been some pracical achievements. However, before the consideration of the estimates has been concluded, we might wish to analyse and discuss some of the particular items to which he referred, and probably raise some questions on matters to which he did not refer.
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) has mentioned one or two of these. There are a number of other matters that are of great concern on the Pacific coast of Canada at the present time to which the minister did not refer. I mention for example the question of licence limitation which is, I think, a matter of great and urgent concern. There is the whole question as to what developments can and should take place in the field of the rights of fishermen in the matter of collective organization, a situation which I think the minister cannot but agree is in a rather unhappy state at the present time in British Columbia because of apparent misunderstandings as to where jurisdiction lies. We have had many unnecessary upsets in the fishing industry in British Columbia due in large part to the fact that there seems to have been no proper exercise of jurisdiction at the government level. Here again the question of federal and provincial jurisdiction seems to enter into it.
The minister in his remarks confined himself almost entirely to what I would call the day-to-day operations of the department and the industry within Canada. But I feel perhaps it might be useful, in the context of our

initial consideration of the estimates of the department for this year, if someone said a few words about the relationship of Canadian fisheries to the situation in the world as a whole. I certainly cannot pose as any authority in this field so I would like, if I may, to draw briefly from what has been said by someone whom I believe-and I think most members will agree with this-is recognized and regarded as an authority in this field. I should like to put on the record one or two quotations from statements which have been made by the recently retired director of the fisheries division of the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations, Dr. D. B. Finn. First of all, Mr. Chairman, if I may I would refer to an article which appeared in the Financial Times of London which the Toronto Globe and Mail thought significant enough to reproduce in June of last year at a time when Dr. Finn was still occupying the post of director of the fisheries division with the United Nations. This statement is as follows:
The most recent statistics show that in 1961 man made his best annual fish catch in history-41,200,000 metric tons.
I suppose these figures are slightly out of date today; the minister indicated that there had been a considerable rise in the last year in the total tonnage of catch in Canadian waters and this may very well apply in some other areas of the world. However, Dr. Finn in his article goes on to point out:
About 80 per cent of this was taken north of the equator, much of it from a few traditionally rich grounds whose names have rung with adventure for centuries-
He goes on to name some of the well known fishing banks adjacent to Europe and adjacent to our eastern shores. He refers to the banks in the East China sea, the Yellow sea and the Kuroshio current, which he says have traditionally supplied the great fish markets of the Far East. Dr. Finn then goes on to say:
But the traditionally good fishing spots are beginning to show signs of depletion. Within the past few years two trends have resulted. First, as resources dwindle, nations have extended their national fishing waters, increasing international problems. Second, fishing is done much farther from home than ever before and catching is combined with processing at sea by the more developed countries.
I believe those remarks are quite significant in view of the fact that, as the minister has indicated, Canadian negotiations in the international field are going on at the present time. While I do not wish to go into that question today in my remarks, nevertheless I make reference to this matter because I

think it points up what some of us in the house have been trying to suggest, namely the urgency and importance of the Canadian government developing satisfactory arrangements with other nations who are interested in the fisheries of the high seas. Dr. Finn in this article goes on to mention another matter. He says:
Two other significant occurrences have influenced fisheries since about 1956. The first is what appears, from slim statistics, to be an upsurge in China's fishing industry. The second is the tremendous growth of the Peruvian fishmeal industry. Peru now catches more than 12 per cent of the entire world catch-a take composed almost entirely of the finger-length anchovy and used almost entirely for animal feed.
The impact of that activity on the part of Peru has not, I think, been without its effect upon certain aspects of the fishing industry on the west coast of Canada. Then Dr. Finn goes on to put our position in perspective with other fishing nations of the world in these words:
In terms of amount of fish caught, the greatest fishing nations rank thus: Japan, China, Peru, Russia, the United States, Norway and Canada. The 1955-59 average catches for the top seven add up to more than half the average total catch of the 73 countries which take 98 per cent of the world catch. In 1959, Britain ranked eighth among fishing nations; in 1961 she ranked eleventh, behind Spain, south and southwest Africa and India.
Part of the explanation for the world catch increase (more than 27 per cent since 1958) lies in today's higher-powered, longer-ranged fishing boats and their modem gear. The largest and most modem of the world's fleets belong to Russia and Japan. Their ships roam almost every sea. Boats of more than 300 horsepower comprised only 6 per cent of the 1960 Soviet fishing fleet, but these boats took 76 per cent of the 1960 Soviet catch.
Then Dr. Finn goes on to describe how both the Japanese and the soviets have developed methods of catching, processing and preserving the fishing products on the high seas in their modern vessels. Later in this article, however, Dr. Finn points out:
Meanwhile, the majority of the world's fishermen still put to sea under oar or sail, many thousands in craft that have undergone few changes since prehistoric times. In large areas of the tropics, one fisherman catches about one ton of fish a year. The rough figure in developed countries is more than 100 tons per man per year.
Despite the far-ranging trawlers, man has not yet made more than a gesture towards exploiting the larger potential of the seas. It is estimated that 90 per cent of sea productivity is never harvested by man.
Since 1955 the Japanese have discovered at least nine new rich tuna areas in the south Pacific and Indo-Pacific. Rich catches are reported from the gulf of Guinea and the north Pacific. The southern seas are virtually untouched.

Dr. Finn then goes on to express his considered opinion in this regard:
The sea can be made to produce more-through species transplantation, for example.
Then he makes reference to the attempt made to transplant Pacific salmon species to the Atlantic coast of Canada and points out that the Soviet union has transferred Baltic herring to the sea of Azov, thereby doubling the growth rate of the species. Later in the article, Dr. Finn suggests-and I quote him again:
Artificially induced upwelling to carry rich seabed nutrients nearer the surface has been proposed to increase fish catches. Slow nuclear reactors lowered into the deeps may, some time in the future, overcome the problem of the tremendous amounts of heat energy required. Direct fertilization especially in narrow bays, may prove successful. Elimination of the major predators of fish would no doubt increase catches. But in this, and in every other instance, the sea's life balance must be preserved and as yet we know too little of these life cycles.
As I said at the outset of my remarks, there might be some virtue, as we discuss the activities of the Department of Fisheries, in making some reference to the position occupied by Canada in relation to world fisheries problems, placing our own situation in total perspective. I should like, if I may, to refer to another article expressing the views of Dr. Finn-an article written shortly after he had retired from his position as director of the fisheries division of the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations. This appeared in the March, 1964 issue of Western Fisheries:
The lack of wise management of the world's fisheries resources seriously restricts man's ability to reap a maximum harvest from the sea, according to Dr. D. B. Finn, who retired January 31 as director of the fisheries division of the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations.
He blamed the inability to get maximum sustained yield from the sea on the intense competitiveness of private fisheries enterprises and the inability of governments to agree on a common code of discipline in exploiting the oceans.
The article goes on to say that Dr. Finn cited the failure of the international whaling convention as one example of this contention. He is then quoted as saying:
The result is that the blue whale is now economically extinct. It seems to me that the world is now on its way to this state of affairs at a rapidly increasing pace.
Private enterprise in fishing tends to become more oligopolistic, if not outright monopolostic. Although this may increase efficiency and make possible a better use of capital, it does nothing to relieve the competition between countries for the spoils of the chase. In fact, it may make it worse.
Nor does increased efficiency in catching, per se, do anything to produce wiser cropping to

Supply-Fisheries
achieve the maximum yield. Under such regimes, the yield of the sea may be far below its potential production. Eventually only the most efficient private expeditions will be able to make fishing pay. This is not necessarily true for state-operated expeditions which may be able to disregard costs as a matter of government policy.
Dr. Finn is then quoted as saying that one of the other problems is the sheer number of organizations now engaged in fisheries research.
In concluding my use of the knowledge and advice of Dr. Finn, I should like to quote the last paragraph of this article. It reads:
Reduced to its simplest terms, world fishing has two elements-the nature of fishing itself, and the living resource and its response to man's exploitation. Describing the first, he said, "Modern fishing is a fiercely competitive hunt. The hunters and their skills increase daily."
I have deliberately introduced the advice and the knowledge contained in these articles because their author, having occupied such an important post for a number of years, is obviously in a much better position to have expert knowledge on the situation than I am, certainly, or indeed any other member of this committee. I think the quotations which I have put on record from these articles place in perspective some of the questions we must consider in relation to our overall fisheries policies. In my view they provide good ground for the concern which all members of this committee should be showing with regard to the results of our efforts in the course of international negotiation-concern, also, that the government of Canada should take seriously the desirability of these negotiations reaching a fruitful outcome.
I think it is apparent, after reading the speeches made during the debate we had earlier when the bill on the fishing zones came before this house, that some of us did not feel the government was taking these matters seriously enough. In fact I sometimes feel the Minister of Fisheries is being left out, in a little corner of his own, away from the centre of government activity. While he may have received some token assistance from our amiable Secretary of State for External Affairs in connection with certain of these negotiations I think the minister and his small complement of officials are left to wrestle with these problems alone, and that the full weight of the government of Canada is not being thrown into these efforts.
The same might be said regarding our attitude toward internal policies. The minister did make some reference to a federal-provincial conference and to this question of a national policy. I listened carefully to his report of some of the activities which, he

said, have already resulted from that conference and I had the feeling, shared apparently by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean), that many of these activities were already in progress, up to a point at least, before that conference began. Representations were made at those meetings, as the minister will recall, to the effect that what we need is a real national development program. Perhaps I may recall some of the statements which were made with particular reference to fisheries problems on the Atlantic coast by someone who is certainly a better authority on these matters than I can claim to be. I refer to the premier of Newfoundland. I had the opportunity of paying a short visit to Newfoundland a few years ago when I saw a little at first hand of the fishing industry in that province. But certainly the presentation made by the premier of Newfoundland to the conference last January is much more up to date than any personal knowledge or impression I have of the situation there.
Perhaps I should point out that in his introduction the premier of Newfoundland had this to say when he presented his statement to the conference on January 20 of this year. I should like to make reference to a few excerpts from the premier's statement. He said:
A year ago the government of Newfoundland made a presentation to the government of Canada -a presentation that we entitled "National fisheries development".
That, of course, was at a time when the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) was still minister of fisheries.
In that presentation we talked of a national fisheries policy as distinct from a Newfoundland fisheries policy. We are still talking about a national policy. And we still visualize the regional and the provincial fisheries programs to be developed within the framework of national policy as integral parts of a broad national, all-Canada, coast to coast fisheries development program.
We are not talking about a policy conceived as a system of welfare payments and handout programs. We are talking about policy designed to achieve far reaching development and investment programs that will enable our Canadian fishermen, whether they be in Newfoundland or Quebec, in Manitoba or in British Columbia to make a decent living from the harvesting of the rich resources of the sea the lakes and the rivers of our land. This is what we ask for Newfoundland. This is what we ask for Canada.
Then in the next paragraph Mr. Smallwood goes on to say:
We do not have it today. Today the position of the fisherman is prejudiced by risk and uncertainty in terms of both price and production. Risk and uncertainty means that capital cannot be safely extended: it means that the organization of co-operatives is fraught with difficulty and

danger. In the distribution of income resulting from the catch the fisherman, certainly the Newfoundland fisherman, is in a residual and untenable position.
A little further on he goes on to say:
Gradually the fish resource becomes little more than a product that marginally reduces the necessity for social and welfare payments. The accumulative effect in the long run is a downward economic spiral of the fishing industry.
Then lastly he points out:
-to this date despite good intentions and a great deal of unco-ordinated piecemeal activity, we have largely failed our fishermen. The fish are there, the markets are there, the fishermen are there. But the governments across Canada have failed to devise that national policy which can provide real opportunities for the men who live by fishing.
I think that these words which were uttered at the beginning of this year may form a fairly sound basis on which we can assess the merits of the statements which were made by the minister in his opening remarks about what progress has been made in the development of a fisheries program.
The minister may recall that the premier's statement was made against the context of a letter which he had received from the present Prime Minister, and perhaps it might be useful to recall what the Prime Minister had to say in this letter to Mr. Smallwood which was apparently written on February 13, 1963. He said:
Dear Mr. Smallwood:
I am grateful to you for giving me a copy of the presentation of the government of Newfoundland to the government of Canada on national fisheries development and for the opportunity, as leader of the Liberal party, to express my attitude to these proposals for a national fishery policy.
While, during an election campaign, I could not possibly secure the expert advice I would require to make a judgment in detail of the various proposals, your approach to a national fishery policy is right in line with the declared policy of the national Liberal party, to "take parallel action for the welfare of farmers and fishermen;" and with the objective set out in my speech on February 11: "to ensure the farmers and the fishermen of all Canada their fair share of the national income and opportunities for a better life".
I have no hesitation, therefore, in undertaking, if I become prime minister after April 8, to submit the Newfoundland proposals to the Department of Fisheries and other agencies of government concerned for immediate examination and report, to be followed promptly by the calling of a federal-provincial fisheries conference to work out a federal-provincial program for fishery development to be founded on the principle that national action for fisheries should parallel the action already being taken, and action to be taken, for agriculture.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) L. B. Pearson

Well, Mr. Chairman, there again I think that in approaching our discussion of these estimates the letter of the present Prime Minister addressed to Premier Smallwood in February 1963 provides a very good basis for us to assess the progress which the minister claims is being made in this respect in his department. The hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) made reference to the fact that we have had some rather important fishery legislation. We had one item, the matter of the 12 mile fishing zone, but I do not see anything on the order paper today with respect to fisheries or fisheries development, any action which has to do with the expansion of fisheries credit, or any of these matters. Had time permitted today during questions I had intended to ask the Prime Minister, knowing that he might have commitments which would make it impossible for him to remain in the chamber during the entire consideration of the fisheries estimates, whether he had anything to add to an answer he gave me on February 21 of this year. As the committee may recall, this was shortly after the Prime Minister had made his opening speech of the current session. I had asked him what measures he had in mind to parallel this action as far as the fishery is concerned-he had made some reference to farm credit in his speech-and the Prime Minister answered in these words, which are to be found at page 92 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I am very conscious of the fact that I did not mention fisheries in my statement yesterday. It was an omission, but I can assure my hon. friend that assistance to agriculture in the form of broadening the basis of farm credit and in other ways will certainly be paralleled by help to the fishery.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, I did not have a chance to ask the Prime Minister today whether he had anything to add to that, and now he is no longer in the house I hope the minister will arrange that the Prime Minister explain when there is going to be this parallel legislation with the farm credit legislation, the farm machinery legislation and some of these other matters which apparently, in the Prime Minister's view and in the view of the premier of the province of Newfoundland, must be part and parcel of an adequate national fisheries development program. In many ways-

I was simply going to say in conclusion that I think it is not unfair to say that in many ways the Department of Fisheries is the Cinderella of the government departments. From what I have been able to observe, so far at least in this session, I must say that the Prime Minister seems to be acting much more in the capacity of the stepmother to Cinderella than in the capacity of the Prince Charming who is going to come along with a golden chariot to assist his minister to carry forward an adequate fisheries development program for Canada.

Mr. Chairman, it is always very interesting to hear a resume of the activities of the fisheries department. I think ministers of fisheries have set a precedent from year to year, and it is now being carried on, in that their introductory remarks have been among the most interesting presented by the ministers of any of the departments. On this occasion the minister has endeavoured to give a fairly comprehensive resume of the work of his department, for which I wish to express our appreciation. I am not going to suggest that the work has been sufficient to meet our expectations and desires, but perhaps we would never be satisfied and would always look for something better and more far reaching. However, we appreciate the statement the minister has made in introducing his estimates.
Reference has been made to the legislation passed recently which extended the territorial seas and fishing limits. The minister is aware that there was considerable dissatisfaction with the extent of the limits provided by that legislation. We were very desirous of having some additions made to the amendments in order to make more real and positive the policies that were expressed and the objectives we desired should be reached. One of those was, of course, a definite setting of the limits or straight base lines. However, we do trust that the minister is pursuing these particular matters with zeal and industry, and we shall look forward in the near future to further statements, we hope setting out the conclusion of negotiations in order to bring into effect what we really desire in this field.
Reference was also made by the minister to discussions currently in progress in respect of the north Pacific treaty, and to the fact that a new draft convention is being discussed.
[The Chairman. 1
We hope in the drafting of this convention the minister has remembered many of those recommendations and representations made by fishermen and fishermen's organizations on the west coast, and I refer particularly to the united fishermen and allied workers union. I believe those recommendations set forth very clearly and positively some of the requirements and needs of the fishing industry in respect of this particular matter. As I have said, I trust the minister will give full consideration to these various representations, and we hope that when the matter is finally resolved it will be to the satisfaction of the fishermen and those who are interested in the fishing industry.
The minister stated that before ratification of the new convention it would be submitted to the committee on marine and fisheries. I do not think this particular committee is being used to its full potential, though during this session the legislation dealing with the 12 mile limit was referred to the committee and considerable discussion was entered into at that time. The committee on marine and fisheries could be used to a much greater extent in an endeavour to resolve some of the fisheries problems, and also to draw public attention to many matters in respect of the fishing industry. A very fine suggestion has been made, that as early as possible in another session the estimates of this department should be submitted for the consideration of the committee on marine and fisheries, and I suggest that whenever it is possible, other matters having to do with fisheries should also be referred to that committee for consideration and recommendation.
The minister referred in his statement to the federal-provincial conference on fisheries development which was held in January of this year. He presented a rather lengthy enumeration of projects under way at the present time, but most of them are, I suggest, of minor consideration. Perhaps that is all we should expect this soon after that conference, but we believe that as time passes, and as additional conferences are held, we will be able to look forward to some very positive legislative action in respect of the fisheries development program. Representatives of various provinces presented recommendations and views in respect of fisheries to the development program, and it would seem to me that we are entitled to expect many of these matters to appear before us in the form of legislation before too long.
The minister's reference to the establishment of regional committees was noteworthy,

as this is a very fine development. We are all aware that in various parts of Canada fisheries problems are different, and it is only natural that in order to arrive at solutions to those problems it will be necessary to deal with them on a more or less regional basis. We recognize the importance of overall national policies in this particular field, as well as in any other field, but to be realistic we also recognize the fact that there are local and regional problems which must be resolved at a local and regional level.
I also noted the minister's reference to the sports fishery advisory council which has been established for British Columbia. It seems that the sports fishery is taking an increasingly important place in the fishing industry, and has been the cause of concern to many individuals who are engaged in commercial fisheries. This has also been a matter of real interest to ardent sports fishermen, and therefore it seems only right and proper that this field of interest or endeavour should be given proper consideration.
I hope the legislation to which the minister referred with regard to seal operations will have the desired effect. We all remember the events of the past, when members of parliament were made aware of the very unfortunate practices being followed in hunting seal. It has been stated that these reports were exaggerated, but it does seem that they were of sufficient interest to cause a great deal of concern across this country, resulting in arousing the concern of a great many people about the activities of those engaged in this operation. We trust that the interest the minister has taken and the legislation he will be proposing will be sufficient to take care of this particular situation.
Mr. Chairman, my remarks are very general today in respect of the first item of these estimates, but as we consider the individual items we will perhaps be taking part in further discussions. However, I am sure we are all aware of the tremendous economic importance of the fishing industry to Canada. It has a particular interest so far as food supplies are concerned, the effects of the industry upon our economy, the employment picture and so on. The fishing industry is indeed one of the major industries of our nation.
Coming as I do from British Columbia I cannot help but concern myself with the fisheries as they affect my own province. I have with me today the British Columbia Government News for July, 1964. This issue brings to our attention some of the relevant 20220-530J
