factors dealing with the different industries of our province and there is a brief statement here regarding fisheries. I should like to place it on the record to show the importance of the fishing industry to my province and, of course, the province of the speaker who preceded me and many others in the house. It reads as follows:
British Columbia fish products in 1963 had a wholesale market value of $76 million. A further $4.1 million in 1963 income is due to halibut landed in United States ports by provincial fishermen and from local processing of imported tuna. Herring production in 1963 reached an all time high. The wholesale marketed value of fish products increased from $57,234,000 in 1952 to $76 million, up 35 per cent, in 1963.
Canada in 1961 ranked sixth in world catch of fish-
According to United Nations statistics.
-and the provincial industry ranks first in Canada in landed and marketed values.
1963 provincial landed catch was worth $38.5 million versus $46.7 million in 1962. About 15,400 commercial licensed fishermen and another 1,250 men were employed on packers and collectors. The 9,746 boats used to land the fish were valued at $70.9 million and gear and shore installations for boats worth $10 million. Landed values were 59 per cent salmon, 15 per cent halibut and 17 per cent herring.
1963 exports of fish and marine products of British Columbia were $42 million, and principal markets were United States, United Kingdom, France, Belgium-Luxembourg, and Australia. Western Europe and United Kingdom took over 50 per cent of foreign shipments.
This points out one of the reasons why I am vitally interested in the fishing industry, and I am sure every member of the house recognizes the importance of this industry not only to our province but to the entire nation. Sometimes I think it is a little difficult for members representing inland constituencies to grasp the significance of the fishing industry and to build up the interest that we would like to see. Nevertheless I am sure that every member is aware of its vast importance to the Canadian economy.
One important aspect of the fisheries program is conservation, and we along the coast of British Columbia are very conscious of the importance of conservation programs and procedures. But while we recognize the importance and necessity, many times we become a little irked at the manner in which the procedures followed are implemented.
The minister is well aware of the fact that in past weeks and months the fishermen of the west coast have been quite disturbed about some of the measures being used and the manner of their application. One area of concern involves the inroads by foreign powers

Supply-Fisheries
into the fishing industry and the fear has been instilled in the minds of the fishermen that the conservation programs being carried on at the expense of Canadian fishermen are possibly being thwarted by concessions being made to foreign fishermen. I know that the fact that these fears have been expressed so often has been a matter of concern to the minister, and I think it would be very useful and advisable that every possible method should be made use of to make the fishermen of the west coast aware of all the factors involved and to make sure that the expenditure of money, as I have said, is not being offset by concessions made to foreign fishermen as opposed to the opportunities that local fishermen enjoy in these particular areas.
Another matter that caused considerable dismay last year was the way in which the closure regulations were applied on the Fraser river. Many fishermen living along the Fraser river depend largely upon the fishing industry for their livelihood, but it almost seems that when the time comes that they can actually make a little money they are faced with closures which make it impossible for them to obtain sufficient income to see them through. Representations were made with regard to this matter, and I would urge that in the implementation of these conservation measures on the Fraser river every possible consideration be given to the local fishermen in order that they may be able to carry on their activities and earn their livelihood from their chosen profession.
Reference was made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni to the matter of licence limitation. This is becoming a very live issue so far as the fishermen of British Columbia are concerned. I do not know to what extent studies have been carried on in this field. I hope the minister will be able to clarify the position of the department with regard to the principle of licence limitation because there is a strong feeling that this is necessary in order to meet the needs of that section of the country. My remarks at this time, Mr. Chairman, are intended to be very general, as I stated, and we shall look forward to taking part in the discussion as we come to the various items in these estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I echo the sentiment expressed by the hon. member for Fraser Valley that it is always a pleasure to taka part in the debate on the estimates of the Minister of Fisheries. This applies today under the present minister and it did under the previous minister, the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean). I believe that mem-

bers cf the house as a whole approach the problems of the fisheries with objectivity and I also believe that not only those members from both coasts of Canada and from the inland fishing areas, but Canadians generally, are aware that the fishing industry is of great importance to Canada and can be and will be, we hope, of even greater importance. As a matter of fact, the intensive expansion of the fishing industry by other nations, many of whose ships appear in the waters off our coast, is an indication of the world wide interest in the fishing industry as mankind strives to find the food that is needed in abundance. Perhaps it is this intensive increase in fishing activity by other nations which provides us with a challenge equally as great as that of the physical needs of the fishermen of Canada. Truly the fishing industry is an industry of great national importance.
Today the minister gave us a very fair resume of the activities of his department and its plans. I am sure all of us appreciate his efforts to supply the committee with the information it requires. I should like to mention one or two matters in my brief remarks. He referred to the failure of the fisheries in Newfoundland, which is in contrast to the fisheries elsewhere in Canada. Unfortunately Newfoundland did not share in the general increase in productivity which the fisheries of other parts of Canada enjoyed. Although we hope that the latter part of the season will partly compensate for the fisheries failure so far, and although increased prices which fortunately exist will help to compensate for this failure and perhaps will go a long way toward compensating for it, nevertheless it is possible there will be areas in Newfoundland in which the catch will be so small the increase in price coupled with an increase in productivity later in the season, will not compensate for the failure of the fisheries in the early part of the season. I would at this point simply ask the minister to keep in mind those fishermen who are so affected.
I should like to direct the minister's attention also to this matter of the poor catch this year, particularly in the cod fishery. It has been suggested that perhaps intensive fishing off the east coast of Canada is responsible for this. I would suggest that this possibility be not overlooked, and as a matter of fact I would suggest serious consideration be given to this contention. Nevertheless I think it fair to point out that these failures in the fisheries do occur from time to time, and

that there does seem to be a cycle with respect to production. I know that in days before there was such intensive fishing by our foreign competitors, such failures did occur. 1 ask the minister to have his department look into this matter of the periodic failure of the fisheries, what they are related to, what part over-fishing may play in them and what part natural cycles have to play in them.
I was interested in hearing the minister say that an extension in the bait service is planned. This is really good news. At the same time, I should like to compliment him on the provision he has made for increases in the stocks of bait when we go into next season's fishing. This is a very important forward step because actually a shortage of bait plagues many sections of Newfoundland. I do think it is desirable that a greater number of bait holding units be supplied, and that it will be necessary to have additional cold storage boat services. I do believe it has been demonstrated that although these small holding units, which are suitable for small fishing communities, are of great value, to supply them effectively additional bait will be needed. I ask the minister to keep this in mind, as well as the possibility of the development of artificial bait for commercial fishing.
I should like to mention that the minister's department should keep in mind the possibility of shipping fish fresh by air from eastern Canada to European markets. I believe there is a great potential there as the standard of living and ability to pay higher prices obtains in Europe. Opportunity will begin to open up for Canada to get into the more lucrative aspects of supplying fresh fish to these markets, because fresh fish brings a much better price than either the frozen article or the salted article.
There is also the possibility of exploiting the turbot fishery to a greater extent. The market for salted turbot is shrinking and an alternative market must be found for turbot in another form such as fresh, or canned, if the turbot fishery is to continue-and we hope it can continue. The fishing industry is the oldest industry in Canada. Like all old industries, it is bound to accumulate many problems as it goes along. I do not believe there is any problem of the fishing industry which is not capable of solution. What is quite frequently referred to as the fishing problem is not so much one great problem as it is the accumulation of several smaller ones which taken individually and examined thoroughly,
Supply-Fisheries
will be capable of solution. In the end this could result in an expansion of this great industry which is essential to Canada and essential to the food supply of the world. The harvest of the sea could well equal in importance the harvest of the land.

It is not my intention to speak at great length and delay the estimates of the Department of Fisheries. However, as the member for Queens-Lunenburg, a riding in which is presently located the largest deep sea fishing fleet in North America, I feel I should make some comments on the problems relating to the fishing industry. I listened with interest to the statement made by the minister and it is evident to me he has made a good start on the fundamental problems faced by his department. It is evident also he inherited a well organized department. I believe we can safely say he has been given the tools, and we know he will accept the responsibility and get on with the job.
Fishing is big business in Nova Scotia. In my province alone the landed value last year represented some $35 million to our fishermen, out of a total landed value in the Atlantic provinces of some $49 million. Canada today is the seventh largest fishing nation in the world. Possessing the world's longest coast line, we are only now beginning to learn something about our continental shelf in areas which have produced such a prolific supply and variety of fish. We are receiving assistance today along this line from the research and development carried out by the oceanographic institute, the first of its kind in Canada, which was opened by the previous administration in 1962 at Bedford basin near Halifax.
While this institute was opened under the direction of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, it still has in it a branch of the fisheries department. As a result, our marine laboratories are expanding; graduate students are being trained in all areas of oceanography and research; new research ships are carrying out scientific investigations along our coasts, the latest being the Canadian scientific ship Hudson, which was under construction since 1961 and which was commissioned on February 14 of this year. A floating laboratory, it is capable of hydrographic and oceanographic work anywhere in the world, but it will perform mainly, I understand, in the Arctic and Atlantic oceans. We can therefore expect rapid development in this field. We are not alone in this work, for all major maritime nations are now taking part. Throughout the world roughly 50 research ships are constantly at sea carrying

Supply-Fisheries
approximately 600 technicians and trained personnel. Through this increase in scientific effort we hope to plug a big gap in our knowledge concerning the earth on which we live. We hope to learn more about the habits of fish which are part of our food resources and which automatically renew themselves.
This study carried on by the department is already producing dividends in the form of a new type of fisheries chart issued by the Canadian hydrographic service to assist fishermen on Canada's east coast to substantially increase their catch. This chart covers Ban-quereau and Misaine banks which lie off Nova Scotia between Scatarie and Sable island. It is essentially an accurate detailed picture of the shape and depth of the sea bottom, enabling fishermen to select the most favourable areas and banks for fishing. It is a good chart. I have had an opportunity to examine it, and it is very well prepared. This of course is a start; but I cannot urge too strongly upon the minister the need for additional charts of this nature covering many other banks off our coasts which are not now clearly outlined and detailed in this manner. With our expanding fishing fleet it is vitally essential that charts of this type be provided to our captains, who are finding it increasingly difficult to secure greater catches of fish, especially at the present time when our offshore banks are being seriously overfished by large trawlers from other nations.
Speaking of trawlers, Mr. Chairman, I think it is important that I bring to the minister's attention the apparent preference by our maritime fishermen for the wooden trawler v. the steel trawler. When the previous administration was in power they instituted the payment of subsidies to encourage the restoration of the shipbuilding industry in Canada. At that time steel ships were subsidized at 50 per cent of the cost of their Canadian content, and wooden ships were subsidized at 40 per cent of the cost of their Canadian content. As a result, the shipbuilding industry today in Nova Scotia is a substantial contributor to the economy of the province. The current boom in Nova Scotia's wooden boat and shipbuilding industry alone is worth more than $10 million a year. All boatyards from Cape Breton island to Yarmouth are operating at maximum capacity. This speaks well for the subsidy policy.
However, the subsidy payment on wooden ships has recently dropped from 40 per cent to 35 per cent, creating a disparity of 15 per cent on subsidy payments between wooden and steel ships. At the same time the costs

of wooden ship construction have been increasing, due in part to recent new tax levies. I would therefore urge upon the Minister of Fisheries that he take steps to remove this discrimination against the wooden ship builder. He may well argue that this matter does not come under his department; that it pertains to transport. But in my view, Mr. Chairman, anything that affects the fishing industry is or should be of vital concern to the Minister of Fisheries.
We have seen many changes in the fishing industry in the last 30 years. When I was a boy growing up in Lunenburg, all deep sea fishing was carried out with dories working from schooners on the banks. It was a tough task, and the list of men and vessels lost at sea in the fishermen's memorial room at the Lunenburg community centre tells the story of disasters at sea in the days of sail in the absence of radio and ship-to-shore communications. In those days a fisherman was lucky if he made $1,000 in a year, and yet they built their homes and raised large families. Today the picture is greatly changed, and the few schooners that are still active in the area have been converted into draggers or long liners. The long-liner is a modification of the earlier form of line fishing from a dory, the only difference being that at the present time it is set from the ship and hauled by an automatic hauler.
Perhaps the greatest innovation in recent years has been the catching of swordfish by using the long line method. Last year's swordfish landings were more than three times greater than in 1962, with a landed value of $21 million. However, though this type of fishing has eliminated the uncertainties of harpooning, it has encouraged more fishermen in 50 or 60 foot boats to travel further out to sea in search of broadbills.
While ranging far from shore they are at the mercy of the elements. This happened on August 3 of this year when the long-liner Cheryl Ann, under the command of Captain Charlie Fevens of Yarmouth, became disabled in a 60 mile an hour gale due to engine failure on Georges bank approximately 120 miles from Yarmouth. The captain radioed the Yarmouth marine radio station requesting help, and a government ship, the Thomas Carleton was dispatched to his assistance. However upon arrival at the scene the captain of the Thomas Carleton advised Captain Fevens that he was not allowed to pull him in but could only stand by so that the crew could be rescued if the fishing boat sank.

Fortunately, a Russian tug was in the area and its captain volunteered immediately to assist and towed the disabled long liner to Yarmouth and safety, free of charge. Apparently the Russians believed in the necessity of protecting the lives of our Canadian fishermen and their ships; and we know from past experience that a similar code exists throughout the United States coastguard, who automatically tow any disabled ships to the nearest port. I would therefore urge the minister to use his authority with his fellow cabinet ministers to bring about changes in the regulations, especially where our fishermen are concerned, so that an incident like the towing of the Cheryl Ann, which is looked upon throughout the east coast as a disgrace to our government services will never occur again.
At this time I wish to again refer to the necessity of bringing about changes in our scallop and lobster fishing regulations. I had previously raised this matter when I spoke in the house on July 8, and it was raised on June 22 when the standing committee on marine and fisheries met to discuss Bill No. S-17, respecting the territorial seas and fishing zones of Canada. I have pointed out that Nova Scotia is the scallop province of Canada, with our ships accounting for at least 98 per cent of all Canadian scallop production. In Lunenburg and Riverport alone we today have 53 large deep sea trawlers, with the majority engaged in catching scallops. In 1963 over 16 million pounds of scallops were landed in Nova Scotia, with a value in excess of $6 million to the fishermen; and the figures will be even higher in 1964. This industry is of tremendous importance, not only to our Nova Scotia fishermen but to the Canadian government, for the bulk of this production is sold to the United States, thus bringing in foreign exchange and needed U.S. dollars. But the Fisheries Act, under clause 31 states, that fish are not to be caught outside territorial waters when catching is forbidden in territorial waters. I was hoping that the minister in his statement would say something that would encourage me and the house to believe that this act would be changed. I will place the words of this section on the records so that hon. members will know just what it implies. Section 31 reads as follows:
No one shall leave any port or place in Canada to fish outside the territorial waters of Canada for fish the catching of which is at such time prohibited in the territorial waters of Canada opposite to or nearest the place where such person proposes to fish, and no one shall bring into Canada any
Supply-Fisheries
fish caught outside the territorial waters of Canada when fishing for such fish is prohibited inside the territorial waters of Canada opposite or nearest to the place where such fish was caught, or shall bring into Canada any vessels, boats, nets, fishing gear, implements or appliances used in such fishing.
If this act were enforced today the scallop fleet operating out of Lunenburg county, could be legally tied up until October 31 thereby creating untold financial hardship in the industry. In my opinion this section of the act not only discriminates against the scallop fishermen but it also prevents the establishment of a deep sea lobster industry in Nova Scotia. As most hon. members are aware, Nova Scotia is divided into lobster fishing zones. Zone four takes in the south shore of Nova Scotia including Lunenburg, Queens, Shelburne, Yarmouth and Digby counties and the fishermen are only permitted to catch lobsters in zone four from December 1 to May 31. During the remaining six months of the year lobsters cannot be caught and legally landed in this area and this applies not only to lobsters caught on the inshore grounds but also to any lobsters which may be caught by deep sea fishermen. Nova Scotia fishermen are thereby prohibited under clause 31 of the Fisheries Act of 1932 from exploiting a deep sea lobster fishery on Georges and Browns banks and also in some areas of the Grand banks, which could be worth over $1 million per year in landed value.
In 1963, the landed value of all fish caught in Nova Scotia amounted to $35 million, a figure which represents an increase of $12 million over a decade ago. Of this total, an estimated 36 million pounds of lobster brought in almost $18 million to our fishermen. Lobsters are therefore the greatest dollar earner for our fishermen with scallops in second place. However, it is evident we are only scratching the surface, for due to prohibitive regulations we are not taking advantage of the opportunities offered by the deep sea lobster industry. We know a great market exists for lobsters both in North America and in Europe. We know that lobster stocks occupy thousands of square miles off our coastal waters, and these could be called our inshore lobster population. We also know that lobsters may be caught in our offshore waters in an area south of Georges bank approximately 100 miles from Yarmouth. What we do not know is the relation between these two lobster populations. Some marine biologists claim there are actually two distinct lobster populations, while others claim that lobsters hatched in the deep waters offshore are carried by strong currents while in the

Supply-Fisheries
free swimming stage and that these lobsters help populate the inshore banks. This is a matter which should receive the attention of scientists in the fisheries department. In my view, common sense tells us that it is wise to carry out conservation measures in our inshore lobster fishery grounds in order to assure relatively good catches and income to our inshore lobster fishermen. However, I question the soundness of carrying out a conservation policy with regard to deep sea lobsters which, in effect, applies only to any potential Canadian deep sea lobster fisherman, while leaving the grounds wide open to fishermen from any other nation wishing to exploit them.
When this question was raised during a discussion in the committee on Bill S-17, the Minister of Fisheries said:
There may be reasons to amend the Fisheries Act. There may be a reason to amend section 31. There may be a reason and a very serious one to amend section 31 of the Fisheries Act to take care of provisions such as the one mentioned by Mr. Crouse. I think the government-and I am sure I can speak in its name-would be prepared to do this if such a need occurred. But I feel it does not affect the present bill. I agree with Mr. Crouse that the government should take into consideration amending section 31 of the Fisheries Act if there is such a need.
Evidently the minister questioned the need for making these changes; he questioned the potential of this industry. In reply, I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Maine Coast Fisherman which states:
Captain Frank Moore, president of the lobster-men's association-
This is in the United States.
-told the committee there were 3,178 lobster licences issued in 1962 for inshore lobstering bringing in $31,780 in revenue to the state.
That is the state of Maine.
He complained that deep sea lobster draggers- a dozen are now working employing about 75 fishermen-are scooping up lobsters from breeding areas offshore. He argued that the deep water breeding areas are the sources of inshore lobsters.
A little further on, the report continues:
He said the offshore lobster business was worth more than $1 million to New Bedford fishermen last year. Latest bureau of commercial fisheries statistics show that the January 1964 catch by lobster draggers totalled 161,000 pounds worth $94,000 compared to 95,000 pounds, valued at $53,000, in the same month of 1963.
I am sure it would be possible to develop a large deep sea lobster industry centered on Georges bank. In fact, speaking in a lighter vein, I think it is necessary to amend these regulations even if only to protect the minister and his staff. I had an opportunity recently

to visit the Nova Scotia fisheries exhibition and there on display was a 28 pound deep sea lobster. When I inquired from a member of the minister's inspection staff where this magnificent lobster had been caught he told me it had been caught on Georges bank and landed at Lunenburg. I said, facetiously of course: "No doubt you will lay charges against the captain who landed this lobster because it has been smuggled into Lunenburg and is illegally on display." The officials laughed and said they hoped this would not be necessary. I tell this story to show that lobsters are being caught and that they are being landed.
I wish to make two proposals to the minister: First, that he bring in an amendment to section 31. If he does so, I can assure him it will receive prompt and speedy passage as far as the official opposition is concerned. Second, I would suggest to the minister that he then equip the A. T. Cameron for lobster dragging for a minimum period of 30 days. This would establish the number of pounds of deep sea lobsters our fishermen could hope to catch and might lead to the establishment of a new industry in Nova Scotia.
I could mention many other items which are also of vital importance, but time will not permit. However, I would specifically mention in closing the necessity for restocking our lakes and rivers with trout and salmon. This would be of great benefit to our tourist industry and any expanded program along these lines would assuredly receive the support of members in all parts of the house.
I hope the minister will give us at a later date a more extensive report on oyster development and the program the department has for restocking the oyster beds. Perhaps he would advise us whether any thought is being given to the artificial breeding and cultivation of clams. I realize the problem is to conserve the clam spat in its early critical stages. Silting, disease, water changes, predators such as starfish all determine the rate of survival of the clam. However, it is evident the Japanese have done great work in this field, and since the raising of clams could provide a supplementary income to our inshore fishermen I hope the minister will give some thought to developing larger stocks of this type of Canadian shellfish.
Progress reported.
